images.caption: Figure 1:Overview of CausGround.CausGround distills open-world interaction experience into reusable action-centered causal knowledge by identifying action preconditions and effects. At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in the current observation to form a local causal graph, supporting backward reasoning over preconditions and forward reasoning over effects for executable long-horizon planning without parameter updates.

Figure 2:Overview of CausGround.Left:CausGround distills interaction trajectories into reusable action-centered causal knowledge by extracting action preconditions and effects, which are organized into generic and instance-specific knowledge.Right:Given the task description and current world state, task-relevant causal knowledge is grounded to construct a causal graph that provides executable guidance for a frozen planner.

Figure 3:Evaluation environments and representative tasks.Left:SWITCH examples covering action selection, error recovery, state verification, and verification action.Right:High-level planning trajectories in RoboCasa and VirtualHome, showing post-action observations. RoboCasa steps correspond to annotated skill stages; VirtualHome uses repaired image observations.
Figure 4:Case Study.Vanilla identifies the correct chair but repeatedly executes SIT without satisfying the NEAR precondition, while CausGround uses causal knowledge to complete the task.
Figure 5:Generalization across model families and scales.CausGround improves SR and final progress across backbones.
Figure 6:Real-world Deployment.Given initial observation and task, CausGround retrieves task-relevant causal knowledge from the interpreted goal state and grounds it to executable actions.

Figure 7:Representative observation repairs in VirtualHome.Each row shows a transition example with the original pre and post observations (left two columns) and the repaired pre/post observations (right two columns).
The repair corrects visually inconsistent state transitions, such as object transfer, container interaction, and posture change, while preserving unrelated scene content.

Figure 8:Representative high-level planning trajectories in RoboCasa.We show five representative tasks covering object manipulation, navigation, container interaction, fixture operation, and multi-step composition.
Each trajectory is represented by intermediate RGB observations and the corresponding high-level actions from our unified action interface.

Figure 9:Representative cases from the selected SWITCH subtasks.We show examples of Action Selection, Recovery, Verification Action, and Verification State.
These subtasks respectively evaluate next-action prediction, error recovery, active verification, and state verification under embodied interactions.

Figure 10:Illustration of the factorized world state.Visual observations are converted into a structured representation that explicitly separates object attributes from inter-object relations.
The same representation is used to describe the current state as well as the preconditions and effects associated with environment interactions.

Figure 11:Illustration of action-centered causal factor identification.CausGround compares executions of the same grounded action under variations of pre-action state factors.
Factors associated with changes in action executability are retained as relevant preconditions, whereas incidental factors that do not affect the execution outcome are discarded.

Figure 12:Task-grounded planning in CausGround.The task description is used to retrieve task-relevant causal knowledge from the CausGround library.
At each planning step, the current observation is converted into a factorized world state and used to ground the retrieved causal graph in the current environment state before action prediction.
The predicted action is executed in the environment, and the resulting observation is returned for the next decision step.

Figure 13:Real-world execution of the microwave task.Given the instruction “Move the bread from the microwave to the plate,” CausGround produces the high-level sequenceOPEN(Microwave)→\rightarrowPICK(Bread)→\rightarrowPLACE(Bread, Plate), which is executed by the robot in the real environment.

Figure 14:Real-world execution of the multi-object task.Given the instruction “Put the banana and bread on the plate,” CausGround sequentially generatesPICK(Banana)→\rightarrowPLACE(Banana, Plate)→\rightarrowPICK(Bread)→\rightarrowPLACE(Bread, Plate), demonstrating multi-object sequential manipulation.
